So Trump gave them something to watch: After pleading ânot guiltyâ to 37 felony counts, he made a surprise visit to famed Cuban restaurant Versailles. Supporters took pictures with him, prayed over him, and even sang âHappy Birthdayâ for his 77th (âsome birthday,â he joked).

He was right âÂ and it was a smart move. On Fox News, which has featured plenty of dour legal takes as well, viewers were suddenly treated to a leader triumphantly surrounded by his fans.
The episode was a preview of where this all is going: The Trump campaign and his legal defense are essentially one and the same.
If there was any doubt, he cleared it up with a rally at Bedminster late that night that stuck to his established playbook.
He conceded nothing: âI did everything right and they indicted me!â he shouted.
He promised retaliation: A âreal special prosecutorâ to investigate Biden and his family, undercutting the Republicans defending him as part of a high-minded stand against the appearance of a partisan Justice Department.

And he went on the attack against his top opponent: âraging lunaticâ Jack Smith.
Trump, who said Smith âlooks like a thugâ and specializes in âpolitical hit jobs,â cited his work on a corruption case against former Virginia Governor Bob McDonnell that the Supreme Court
overturned
in a landmark ruling. His approach was all but indistinguishable from the treatment he gave various presidential rivals, right down to targeting Smithâs wife.
The closest Trump came to directly acknowledging the seriousness of the charges heâs facing was a riff on the Espionage Act, which he said âhas been used to go after traitors and spiesâ and should not apply to him (the relevant charges are
not about spying
and donât need to be, though there are critics of the
broader law
in that regard).
By the end of the speech, the line between his presidential and legal campaign had disappeared entirely: âOn November 5, 2024, justice will be done, we will take back our country, and we will make America great again,â he said.

There are risks to this approach. Trumpâs words can and will be used against him in a court of law, and potentially undercut his lawyersâ strategy (though they vetted his speech, an aide said). He received a reminder of that on Tuesday, when a judge allowed E. Jean Carroll to amend her defamation lawsuit âÂ which already resulted in a $5 million jury decision against him âÂ to include his
more recent comments
lashing out at her.
But Trumpâs also not a normal defendant. He can win the White House and pardon himself. He can bully his rivals into promising to do the same âÂ one of them, Vivek Ramaswamy, has already done so, while Nikki Haley, who has criticized Trumpâs conduct, said she was
âinclined in favorâ
of a pardon given her discomfort at the idea of a jailed former president. He can hope the judge he personally appointed, who was
excoriated by a circuit court
that determined she lent him special treatment in prior rulings, is also uneasy with trying him like a typical accused felon.
Finally, Trump can also hope that the case heâs making daily â that heâs a victim of a partisan witch hunt â seeps into the public, where the court has to
find jurors
who somehow arenât tainted by the news surrounding the most famous and polarizing figure in the country. Those restaurant-goers watching him work the crowd? Any one of them could end up in a jury pool.
